title: The Wolf, the Fox, and the Ape
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Wolf charged a Fox with theft, which he denied, and the case was brought before an Ape to be tried. When he had heard the evidence on both sides, the Ape gave judgment as follows: "I do not think," he said, "that you, O Wolf, ever lost what you claim; but all the same I believe that you, Fox, are guilty of the theft, in spite of all your denials." The dishonest get no credit, even if they act honestly.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Wolf charge the Fox with?
According to the passage, what did the Fox do when charged with theft?
According to the passage, before whom was the case brought to be tried?
According to the passage, what did the Ape do before giving judgment?
options: He heard the evidence on both sides
He delayed the trial a day

questions.prompt: According to the Ape's judgment, what does he say about the Wolf's claim?
options: That the Wolf exaggerated the value of what was lost
That the Wolf never actually lost what he claimed
That the Wolf stole it back himself
That the Wolf's claim could not be judged fairly

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "denials" mean in "in spite of all your denials"?
options: Statements refusing to admit something is true

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what is unusual about the Ape's verdict?
options: He punishes the Wolf instead of the Fox
He refuses to rule on the case at all
He declares the Wolf never lost anything, yet still finds the Fox guilty of stealing it
He asks both animals to apologize to each other

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: A known liar is not believed even when telling the truth
Apes make the fairest judges of any animal
Wolves are more trustworthy than foxes in court
Every accusation of theft should be dismissed without evidence

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who denied the charge of theft?
According to the passage, what exact words does the Ape use to open his judgment?
According to the Ape's judgment, what does he conclude about the Fox despite his denials?
options: That the Fox is guilty of the theft
That the Fox should be released without charge
That the Fox deserves a lighter punishment
That the Fox's case should be retried

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "charged" mean in "A Wolf charged a Fox with theft"?
Based on the passage's closing line, why might the Ape have ruled against the Fox despite the Wolf having lost nothing?
options: The Fox's known dishonesty made his denials worthless in the Ape's eyes
The Ape wanted to please the Wolf regardless of the facts
The Fox admitted guilt partway through the trial
The evidence clearly proved the Fox had taken something

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: An Ape judges a theft case and rules that the Wolf lost nothing, yet the Fox is still guilty
A Wolf and a Fox settle their dispute without a trial
An Ape is put on trial for stealing from both the Wolf and the Fox
The Fox proves his innocence and the Wolf is punished instead
